title: Decline in insect populations

definition.text: The widespread fall in insect numbers across many insect groups, reported since the 2010s, sometimes extending to species extinction.

facts.text: Insects account for up to 90% of all animal species.
Estimates of insect species at risk of extinction range from 10% to 40%.
A 2020 meta-analysis of 166 long-term studies found land insects declining about 9% per decade, while freshwater insects rose 11% per decade.
Causes ranked by one study: habitat loss to intensive farming and cities, pollution from pesticides and fertilisers, pathogens and introduced species, then climate change.
A German study found a 76% seasonal decline in flying insect biomass in nature reserves over 1989–2016.
The decline threatens insect-eating birds and mammals and services such as crop pollination and waste disposal.
Global trends are hard to infer because data vary by time, place and species and are concentrated in Western Europe and North America.

related: Agriculture as a driver of biodiversity loss
contested_note: A 2019 review's projection that 40% of insect species could go extinct within decades was challenged, and global estimates remain uncertain.

title: Wildflower strips
article: Decline in insect populations#Wildflower strips and buffer zones

definition.text: Strips of land at field edges sown with pollinator-friendly flowering plants to support insects and farmland wildlife.

facts.text: They aim to sustain local biodiversity, conserve insects, restore farmland birds and offset the harms of agricultural intensification.
Pesticide-reduced buffer zones around nature reserves have also been proposed, after a German study found insects there carried about 16 pesticides on average.

title: Desertification

definition.text: The gradual degradation of fertile land in dry regions into desert, through natural processes and human activities.

facts.text: Its immediate cause is the loss of most vegetation, driven by drought, climate shifts, tillage, overgrazing and cutting trees for fuel or building.
Bare dry soil blows or washes away, leaving infertile layers that bake into unproductive hardpan.
Drylands cover about 40–41% of Earth's land and are home to more than 2 billion people, at least 90% of them in developing countries.
Some 10–20% of drylands are already degraded, and a billion people are threatened by further desertification.
Climate change is expected to expand drylands from 38% of continental land in the late 20th century to 50% or 56% by 2100.
Sustainable practices can cost individual farmers more than they gain even when they benefit society and the environment.
Shelter belts, woodlots and windbreaks are used to fix soil and cut erosion.

related: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification

title: Desertification causes debate

definition.text: The dispute over how much local overgrazing and farming, rather than climate, drive desertification.

facts.text: Early studies blamed overgrazing by livestock as a leading cause.
Sahel drought is now thought to stem mainly from rainfall variability driven by ocean temperatures, aerosols and greenhouse gases.
Changing ocean temperatures and lower sulfate emissions re-greened the Sahel, leading some scholars to call farming-induced vegetation loss a minor factor.
By 2005 there were more than 100 formal definitions of desertification.

contested_note: Researchers disagree on whether local overexploitation or climate variability is the main recent driver of desertification.
